blocks.text: Atomic spectra provide evidence for quantised photons. The experimental arrangement consists of a discharge tube, a spectrometer and a diffraction grating (Fig 18.9): light from the source passes through a narrow slit and a collimator, which makes it parallel, falls on the grating, and is viewed through a rotating telescope. A series of bright lines is seen on a dark background. The vapours of different elements give different patterns of lines, called spectral series, which can be used to identify elements.

blocks.alt: A top view of a grating spectrometer: a lamp and a narrow slit, a collimator tube that makes the light parallel, a diffraction grating standing on a turntable with an angle scale, and a telescope with an eyepiece that rotates about the table. Parallel light leaves the grating at an angle theta to the straight-through direction and enters the telescope. A note gives d sin(theta) = n lambda.
blocks.caption: A diffraction grating spectrometer (original diagram after Fig 18.9).
blocks.long_description: Each wavelength in the light is diffracted to its own angle, so turning the telescope brings the lines of the spectrum into view one by one against a dark background, and their angles are read on the scale.

blocks.text: One such series was identified by J. J. Balmer in 1885 in the spectrum of atomic hydrogen (Fig 18.10). In the visible region it has four lines, at 656 nm (red), 486 nm (blue-green), 434 nm (blue) and 410 nm (violet). J. R. Rydberg expressed the results in the formula 1/lambda = RH (1/2^2 - 1/n^2), where n = 3, 4, 5, ... is the excited energy level of the electron and RH = 1.0974 x 10^7 m^-1 is the Rydberg constant. The spectral lines of hydrogen also extend into the invisible ultraviolet and infrared regions. In the ultraviolet, the Lyman series is given by 1/lambda = RH (1/1^2 - 1/n^2), n = 2, 3, 4, ... (18.12). In the infrared, the Paschen series is given by 1/lambda = RH (1/3^2 - 1/n^2), n = 4, 5, 6, ... (18.13).

These equations give the allowed energies of the electron in an isolated hydrogen atom (Figs 18.11 and 18.12). The state n = 1 is the ground state; n = 2, 3, 4, ... are excited states. An atom absorbs energy only in discrete amounts and is raised to one of its excited states. Excited states are very short-lived: the electron soon returns to a lower level, emitting a photon, and these photons form the emission spectrum of spectral lines. Transitions ending on n = 1 give the Lyman series, those ending on n = 2 the Balmer series, and those ending on n = 3 the Paschen series.

blocks.alt: Top: a dark strip with four coloured lines of the Balmer series at 410, 434, 486 and 656 nm, violet on the left and red on the right. Bottom: an energy-level diagram for hydrogen with levels n = 1 (-21.8), 2 (-5.45), 3 (-2.42), 4 (-1.36), 5 (-0.86), 6 and infinity (0), in units of 10^-19 J. Downward arrows to n = 1 form the Lyman series (UV), coloured arrows to n = 2 the Balmer series (visible), and arrows to n = 3 the Paschen series (IR).
blocks.caption: Spectra of atomic hydrogen and its energy levels (original diagram after Figs 18.10 to 18.12).
blocks.long_description: Each line comes from one jump between two levels; the bigger the jump, the more energetic the photon. Jumps to n = 1 are the largest (ultraviolet); jumps to n = 2 happen to fall in the visible range.

blocks.text: When light with a continuous spectrum, such as white light, passes through a gas at low pressure and is then analysed, light of certain wavelengths is found to be missing; dark lines appear in their places. This is an absorption spectrum. As the light passes through the gas, electrons absorb discrete amounts of energy and move to higher levels; only photons of certain energies are absorbed, exactly those needed for such upward transitions. When the excited electrons return to lower levels, photons of those same wavelengths are emitted, forming the emission spectrum. So the wavelengths missing from an absorption line spectrum are those present in the emission line spectrum of the same element (Fig 18.13).

blocks.title: Do you know?
blocks.text: To excite an atom, a photon must have energy exactly equal to the energy difference between two levels, hf = En - Ep. An electron striking the atom, however, can excite it if its kinetic energy is greater than or equal to that difference. The different types of spectra are continuous, line and band.

blocks.alt: Three strips against wavelength from 400 to 700 nm. Continuous: a full rainbow from violet to red. Hydrogen emission: a dark strip with bright coloured lines at 410, 434, 486 and 656 nm. Hydrogen absorption: the rainbow with dark lines at exactly the same four wavelengths.
blocks.caption: Continuous, emission and absorption spectra (original diagram after Fig 18.13).
blocks.long_description: A gas absorbs exactly the wavelengths it can emit, because both come from jumps between the same pairs of energy levels.
